Speech-Language Therapy & Communication

Speech-Language Therapy & Communication

THERAPIST SPOTLIGHT

How speech-language pathologists help autistic and ADHD people connect and be understood.

Speech-language pathologists, often called SLPs or speech therapists, support every form of communication: understanding, expressing, social interaction and literacy. This deck covers what they do for autistic people and people with ADHD.

What an SLP works on

Language

Social communication

Speech & AAC

Understanding words and sentences, and expressing needs and ideas.

Clear speech, plus pictures, signs or devices when helpful.

Conversation, turn-taking and reading context, on the person's terms.

SLPs assess receptive language (understanding) and expressive language (saying). Social communication work should teach skills the person finds useful, and should respect autistic communication styles rather than forcing eye contact or scripted small talk. They also support speech sound clarity and introduce augmentative and alternative communication.

All communication counts: speech, signs, pictures, devices and behavior.

Every person deserves a reliable way to be heard.

KEY IDEA

Some autistic people speak fluently, some speak a little, some do not speak, and many lose speech under stress. Behavior is communication too. The SLP's job is to make sure the person has a dependable way to share needs, opinions and feelings at all times.

AAC: another way to talk

Myth: AAC stops speech

Research shows AAC does not hold back speech, and it can support speech development. It also reduces frustration.

Picture boards and communication books

Speech-generating apps and devices

Sign language and gestures

Useful for full-time or part-time use

AAC stands for augmentative and alternative communication. It ranges from simple picture cards to sophisticated speech-generating devices. A persistent myth is that AAC prevents people from learning to speak; studies do not support this, and AAC often supports spoken language. Many speaking autistic adults also use AAC when tired or overwhelmed.

How SLPs help with ADHD

Following directions

Storytelling & writing

Conversation flow

Reading comprehension

Strategies for multi-step instructions and listening.

Organizing ideas into a clear beginning, middle and end.

Turn-taking, staying on topic and repairing misunderstandings.

Tracking main ideas and details in longer texts.

Children with ADHD are more likely to have language and learning differences. SLPs help with working-memory heavy tasks such as following directions, with narrative and written organization, and with the pragmatics of conversation. Visual supports and graphic organizers are common tools.

Support communication at home

Model

Wait

Respond

Expand

Use words, signs or AAC yourself.

Pause longer than feels natural.

Honor every attempt to communicate.

Add one word to what they said.

1

2

3

4

Family members are the most important communication partners. Modeling means using the person's system yourself, without demanding they repeat it. Waiting gives processing time. Responding to every attempt shows communication works. Expanding gently grows language: if a child says 'car', you might say 'red car'.

Key takeaways

SLPs support every form of communication, not just speech.

1

AAC is a valid way to talk, and it does not stop speech.

2

Everyday conversations at home multiply therapy gains.

3

Summarize: communication is a right, AAC is a tool, families are partners. In the U.S., SLPs are licensed by their state and certified by ASHA, shown as CCC-SLP.
